proof:
# Equality and strictness in arithmetic and concave-root tail concavity

Throughout, d is a real number at least one, D=d+1, and p=1/D.
All sequence entries under discussion are strictly positive on their
actual, finite, consecutive index interval. The concavity theorem is
proved in `candidate 821242aee5d2f3e1`; this note gives its
complete equality classification. No mixed-integer depth theorem is
asserted.

## 1. Exact classification for arithmetic partial sums

For rho>0 put

    A_m=sum_(j=0)^m(rho+j)^d,    m=0,1,2,... .

At every actual interior node m>=1,

    A_(m+1)^p+A_(m-1)^p <= 2A_m^p.                    (1)

If d>1, the inequality is always STRICT. If d=1, equality at even one
node occurs if and only if rho=1/2. At that shift every node is an
equality and A_m^(1/2)=(m+1)/sqrt(2).

### Strictness of the increment function when d>1

Define f_x(s)=(x+s)_+ for 0<=s<=1. The increment function is

    g(x)=[(x+1)_+^D-x_+^D]^(1/d)
         =D^(1/d)||f_x||_(L_d[0,1]).

For distinct x,y>-1, the two nonzero functions f_x,f_y are not
proportional almost everywhere. If either argument is negative, their
positive supports differ on a set of positive measure unless both
arguments are nonnegative. In the latter case proportionality of the
affine functions x+s and y+s forces equality of their slopes and then
x=y. The same argument covers an argument equal to zero.

The L_d norm is strictly convex for d>1: after normalizing two functions
to norm one, strict convexity of the scalar power t->|t|^d proves a
strict norm inequality unless the functions agree almost everywhere.
Equivalently, the triangle inequality is strict for two nonzero
nonproportional nonnegative functions. Combining this fact with the
pointwise positive-part inequality gives, for 0<theta<1,

    g((1-theta)x+theta y)<(1-theta)g(x)+theta g(y)

whenever x,y>-1 are distinct. Thus g is strictly convex on (-1,infinity).

### Applying strictness to the arithmetic proof

The initial-triple proof in the cited note writes

    U_0=A_0^p, U_1=A_1^p, delta=U_1-U_0>0, t=U_0/delta>0,
    rho=delta^(D/d)t^(D/d),
    rho+1=delta^(D/d)g(t).

Since t-1>-1, strict convexity gives

    g(t+1)>2g(t)-g(t-1)>=2g(t)-t^(D/d).

The second inequality uses g(t-1)<=t^(D/d), valid also for t<1.
Consequently A_2^p<2A_1^p-A_0^p: the first triple is strict.

For precision about propagation, let B(q), q>1, be the unique positive
equality barrier from the cited note:

    (B+(q+1)^d)^p+(B-q^d)^p=2B^p,    B>q^d.

On F>=q^d the associated left-minus-right expression is strictly
negative for F<B(q), zero at B(q), and positive for F>B(q). The
equality-barrier proof writes its three roots as U-delta,U,U+delta,
with x=U/delta>1, and has

    q=delta^(D/d)g(x-1),   q+1=delta^(D/d)g(x).

Strict convexity on [x-1,x+1] makes its next-step inequality strict:

    B(q+1)>B(q)+(q+1)^d.                               (2)

The initial strict triple gives A_1<B(rho+1). Induction with (2)
gives A_m<B(rho+m) at every m>=1. The barrier's strict sign statement
then gives the strict version of (1) at every node.

### The complete d=1 calculation

For d=1 the sum has the exact formula

    A_m=(m+1)(rho+m/2)
        =[(m+rho+1/2)^2-(rho-1/2)^2]/2.               (3)

If rho=1/2, its square root is the affine function claimed above.
Otherwise, extend the expression to real m>=0. Its second derivative is

    -(rho-1/2)^2 /
      {sqrt(2)[(m+rho+1/2)^2-(rho-1/2)^2]^(3/2)}<0.

The radicand is positive because rho>0. Strict continuous concavity
therefore gives strict concavity at every integer midpoint. This proves
the entire arithmetic classification.

## 2. Complete classification for arbitrary positive concave-root sequences

Let a_l,...,a_r>0, suppose h_j=a_j^(1/d) is a concave sequence, and put

    F_i=sum_(j=i)^r a_j.

For each actual interior node l<i<r consider

    F_(i-1)^p+F_(i+1)^p<=2F_i^p.                       (4)

If d>1, (4) is always STRICT.

If d=1, equality holds at i if and only if the entire suffix beginning
at its predecessor has the form

    a_j=(2(r-j)+1)a_r,       j=i-1,...,r.              (5)

Equivalently, this suffix is a strictly decreasing arithmetic sequence
whose final term is half its positive decrement. The decrement is
necessarily 2a_r; it is not an independently adjustable parameter.

### Reduction to a strictly decreasing arithmetic envelope

At the node i write F=F_i, A=a_(i-1), b=a_i. If A<=b, the strict
concavity of t^p gives

    (F+A)^p+(F-b)^p
       <2[(2F+A-b)/2]^p<=2F^p,

since F+A and F-b are distinct and nonnegative. Thus equality requires
A>b. Set

    delta=A^(1/d)-b^(1/d)>0,  q=b^(1/d)/delta.

Concavity of h and positivity of a_(i+1) imply q>1. They also give
the termwise upper bounds

    a_(i+k)<=delta^d(q-k)_+^d

for every available k>=0. Extend the left side by zero after r for
this comparison only, and put

    F_max=delta^d S_d(q),
    S_d(q)=sum_(k>=0)(q-k)_+^d.

Then b<F<=F_max. Section 1 implies the arithmetic midpoint inequality
at F_max, strictly when d>1. The strict-concave function

    h(s)=(1+As)^p+(1-bs)^p-2

has strictly decreasing secant slope h(s)/s for s>0, with h(0)=0.
As 1/F>=1/F_max, this gives two exact consequences:

* If the arithmetic inequality at F_max is strict, the one at F is
  strict as well.
* If it is an equality, equality at F is possible only when F=F_max.

The first consequence proves the complete d>1 assertion.

### Necessity and sufficiency when d=1

By Section 1, equality for the arithmetic tail S_1(q) requires

    q=m+1/2 for an integer m>=1.

Equality at the actual node additionally requires F=F_max. Every
termwise envelope deficit is nonnegative, so this equality of sums
forces equality in every term. The positive envelope terms are exactly
k=0,...,m. The actual positive suffix must therefore end at r=i+m,
and

    a_(i+k)=delta(m+1/2-k),  k=0,...,m.

In particular a_r=delta/2. The defining predecessor relation
A=b+delta gives the same formula at j=i-1. This proves (5).

Conversely, suppose (5) holds and put m=r-i>=1. Summing the odd
integers gives

    F_(i-1)=a_r(m+2)^2,
    F_i=a_r(m+1)^2,
    F_(i+1)=a_r m^2.

Their square roots form an arithmetic progression, proving equality
in (4). This completes both directions without any approximation.

## 3. Exact d=1 defect and the pattern of all equality nodes

The previous classification has a useful quantitative expression.
Assume d=1 and A>b at an interior node. Set delta=A-b, q=b/delta>1,
and write q=m+rho with m>=1 and rho in (0,1]; use rho=1 for integer q.
Define the algebraic barrier

    F_*=(A+b)^2/[8(A-b)]
        =(delta/2)(q+1/2)^2.

The arithmetic envelope has the exact deficit identity

    F_*-F
      =(delta/2)(rho-1/2)^2+(F_max-F).                (6)

Both terms are nonnegative. The first measures the fractional-shift
defect, and the second is the sum of the missing arithmetic-envelope
masses. Equation (6) follows directly from (3) applied to S_1(q).

There is also an exact formula for the midpoint concavity gap:

    2sqrt(F)-sqrt(F+A)-sqrt(F-b)
      =8delta(F_*-F) /
       { [2sqrt(F)+sqrt(F+A)+sqrt(F-b)]
         [2F-delta+2sqrt((F+A)(F-b))] }.              (7)

To verify it, rationalize the first difference and then rationalize
2F-delta-2sqrt((F+A)(F-b)). The resulting numerator is
(A+b)^2-8delta F. Both denominator factors are strictly positive:
q>1 implies b>delta and F>b. Thus (6)-(7) give an exact, nonasymptotic
rigidity certificate for d=1.

For a fixed finite concave sequence, its equality nodes form either
the empty set or a terminal consecutive block of its actual interior
indices. Indeed equality at i forces (5), which in turn forces the
same condition at every later interior node. In particular, equality
at any node requires the last three masses to be in the ratio 5:3:1.
That ratio alone guarantees equality at the last interior node; earlier
equalities require the corresponding longer odd-integer suffix.

If the sequence has at least three entries, equality at EVERY interior
node is equivalent to the full profile

    a_j=(2(r-j)+1)a_r,       j=l,...,r.                (8)

Earlier entries outside an equality-forcing suffix need only satisfy
the original positivity and concavity assumptions. They need not
continue the same arithmetic line. For example

    (15/2,7,5,3,1)

is concave, is strict at its first interior tail-root node, and has
equality at its last two interior nodes.

## 4. Actual endpoints, zero extensions, and integer means

If the support has one or two entries, it has no actual interior node;
the statements about all such nodes are vacuous. Formula (8) is asserted
only when the support has at least three entries.

The artificial tail endpoint F_(r+1)=0 is NOT part of the preceding
concavity classification. A comparison centered at r, if separately
requested, is governed solely by

    (a_(r-1)+a_r)^p<=2a_r^p,

and hence is equivalent to

    a_(r-1)<=(2^(d+1)-1)a_r.

Equality is possible at that artificial comparison in every dimension.
For example the three positive masses (A,A,1), with
A=2^(d+1)-1, have concave d-th roots and equality at this artificial
last node, while their only actual interior node is strict. Increasing
A makes the artificial inequality fail, still with concave d-th roots.

Similarly, if one artificially sets A_(-1)=0 for the arithmetic sums,
the comparison centered at m=0 is an equality exactly at

    rho=1/[(2^(d+1)-1)^(1/d)-1].                       (9)

It holds strictly for larger rho and fails for smaller rho. Equation
(9) reduces to rho=1/2 for d=1; for d>1 it is an extra endpoint
phenomenon and does not contradict strictness at every m>=1.

Finally, normalize a positive finite concave-root sequence to total
mass one and suppose its mean is an integer. The sharp closed-tail
bound gamma_(d+1) is NEVER attained by such a finite sequence: the
upper-endpoint integral partition in the tail proof is strictly larger
than integral_0^1 t^p dt on every interval of positive mass. A singleton
has closed-tail mass one, also strictly greater than gamma_(d+1).

There is additional rigidity in the Jensen step for a nonsingleton
integer-mean sequence. Its support has at least three entries, since
a positive distribution on two consecutive integers has a noninteger
mean. When d>1 all interior tail-root nodes are strict. When d=1,
the fully affine profile (8), with N=r-l+1 entries, has mean

    l+(N-1)(2N-1)/(6N).                                (10)

For N>1 this is not an integer: integrality would imply that N divides
(N-1)(2N-1), but this product is congruent to one modulo N. Therefore
an integer-mean nonsingleton sequence has at least one strict interior
tail-root node even for d=1. Its positive weights on the full index
interval then make the concave-interpolation Jensen inequality strict.
The limiting sharpness constructions in the original theorem are
consistent with all these finite strictness statements; no uniform
positive gap is claimed.
